e.etymology: English form of Welsh Owain, probably from Latin Eugenius, 'well-born', and also of Irish Eoghan. Owain Glyndwr led the last great Welsh revolt against English rule.
From Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious', through Greek Ioannes and Latin Iohannes. The name of John the Baptist and the apostle John, and for centuries the most common English boys' name.

assoc.t: the john, slang for a toilet
a john, slang for a prostitute's customer
John Doe, the placeholder name for an unknown man

e.note: In American slang a john is a toilet and also a prostitute's customer.

e.meaning: man from Lucania; also linked to Latin lux, light
e.etymology: Italian form of Luke, from Latin Lucas and Greek Loukas, 'man from Lucania' in southern Italy. English speakers borrowed it in the 2000s.

assoc.t: the sea monster boy of Pixar's 2021 film Luca

e.etymology: From a Scottish surname taken from a place in Ayrshire, from Gaelic lagan, 'little hollow'. It has been a first name since the 19th century.

assoc.t: Wolverine of the X-Men, hero of the 2017 film Logan
Logan International Airport in Boston

e.etymology: From the English and Scottish occupational surname for a harp player. Its best-known bearer is Harper Lee, author of To Kill a Mockingbird; use for girls rose quickly in the 2000s and 2010s.
namesakes: Harper Lee (author of To Kill a Mockingbird)

assoc.t: Harper Lee, author of To Kill a Mockingbird
Harper's Bazaar fashion magazine
Harper, the book imprint of HarperCollins

e.etymology: From Latin luna, 'moon'. Luna was the Roman goddess of the moon, and the same word means moon in Spanish and Italian.

assoc.t: Luna Lovegood of the Harry Potter series
Luna nutrition bars
luna moth, the large pale green moth

e.note: Also one of the most popular names for dogs and cats in the US.

e.etymology: The spelling of Sophia used in Spanish, Italian, Portuguese and the Scandinavian languages, from Greek sophia, 'wisdom'. Also the name of Bulgaria's capital city.

assoc.t: Sofia, capital of Bulgaria
Disney Junior's princess in Sofia the First

e.etymology: From the English surname meaning 'son of Jack'. Americans began using it as a first name in the 19th century, the era of President Andrew Jackson.

assoc.t: Michael Jackson, the King of Pop (surname)
President Andrew Jackson, on the $20 bill (surname)
Jackson, Mississippi, and Jackson Hole, Wyoming

e.etymology: From Hebrew Yosef, 'he will add', Rachel's wish for another son. The name of Jacob's favored son, sold into Egypt by his brothers, and of the husband of Mary.
namesakes: Saint Joseph (husband of Mary in the Gospels)
Joe Biden, born Joseph (46th US president)

e.etymology: Spanish and Portuguese form of Camilla, from Latin camilla, a girl of noble birth who assisted at religious rites. In Virgil's Aeneid, Camilla is a swift warrior maiden.
From the English occupational surname for a stonemason, from Old French macon.

assoc.t: mason jar, the glass canning jar
Mason, a member of the Freemasons

e.etymology: From Hebrew Dawid, 'beloved'. The shepherd who killed Goliath and became the second king of Israel; also the patron saint of Wales.
namesakes: King David (biblical king who slew Goliath)

assoc.t: Michelangelo's statue of David
David sunflower seeds
David's Bridal, wedding dress chain

e.etymology: From an English surname based on Averay, the Norman French form of Alfred, from Old English aelf, 'elf', plus raed, 'counsel'. Once a boys' name, it has gone mostly to girls since the 2000s.

assoc.t: Avery labels and office supplies

e.etymology: From Latin Iulianus, 'of Julius', the Roman family name of Julius Caesar. A 4th-century Roman emperor and several early saints carried it.
namesakes: Julian Lennon (musician, son of John Lennon)

assoc.t: Julian calendar, introduced by Julius Caesar

e.etymology: The Greek form of Elijah, from Hebrew Eliyahu, 'Yahweh is my God'. It is the prophet's name in the New Testament and in many European languages.

e.meaning: great tide, son of the sea
e.etymology: From Welsh elements usually read as 'great tide' or 'son of the sea'. In the Mabinogion, Dylan is a sea-born hero. Poet Dylan Thomas and singer Bob Dylan spread it abroad.

assoc.t: Bob Dylan, singer-songwriter (stage surname)

e.meaning: man from Lucania; also linked to Latin lux, light
e.etymology: English form of Latin Lucas, from Greek Loukas, 'man from Lucania' in southern Italy. Luke was the physician credited with the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles.

assoc.t: Luke Skywalker of Star Wars
Gospel of Luke in the New Testament

e.etymology: From Hebrew Mattityahu, 'gift of the Lord', through Greek Matthaios and Old French Mathieu. Matthew was the tax collector turned apostle credited with the first Gospel.

assoc.t: Gospel of Matthew, first book of the New Testament
Hurricane Matthew, which hit Haiti and the Carolinas in 2016

e.etymology: From Hebrew Yaakov, tied to akev, 'heel': Jacob is born gripping his twin Esau's heel, and the name came to be read as 'supplanter'. He is the father of the twelve tribes of Israel.

assoc.t: Jacob Black, the werewolf of the Twilight saga

e.etymology: From Provencal Alienor, first borne by Eleanor of Aquitaine (1122-1204), queen of France and then of England. One theory reads it as 'the other Aenor', after her mother; the meaning is not settled.
namesakes: Eleanor of Aquitaine (medieval queen of France and England)

assoc.t: Eleanor Rigby, the Beatles song
Eleanor, the Mustang in Gone in 60 Seconds

e.etymology: From an English surname based on the medieval name Wyot, from Old English Wigheard: wig, 'war', plus heard, 'brave, hardy'. Lawman Wyatt Earp gave it a Western flavor.
namesakes: Wyatt Earp (Old West lawman of the O.K. Corral gunfight)

e.etymology: From the English occupational surname for someone who hauled goods by cart. As an Irish surname it can also come from Mac Artuir, 'son of Arthur'.

assoc.t: Carter's baby and children's clothing
President Jimmy Carter (surname)

e.etymology: From Hebrew Elisheva, 'my God is an oath', through Greek Elisabet. In the Gospels she is the mother of John the Baptist; two long-reigning English queens kept the name in constant use.
namesakes: Queen Elizabeth II (British monarch for 70 years)

assoc.t: Elizabeth, New Jersey

e.etymology: From Hebrew Gavri'el: gever, 'strong man', plus El, 'God'. The archangel who announces the births of John the Baptist and Jesus.
A respelling of Aidan, the English form of Irish Aodhan, a diminutive of Aodh, 'fire', the name of a Celtic sun god. This spelling overtook the original in the US in the 2000s.
e.note: Part of the 2000s wave of rhyming -aden names (Jayden, Brayden, Caden), so classrooms may hold several.

e.etymology: From the English word maverick, 'an unbranded calf', then 'an independent person', after Texas rancher Samuel Maverick, who left his cattle unbranded. The surname itself is of uncertain origin.
namesakes: Bret Maverick (gambler hero of the TV Western Maverick)

assoc.t: Maverick, Tom Cruise's pilot in Top Gun
maverick, the word for an independent-minded person
Ford Maverick pickup truck

e.etymology: From an English surname meaning 'son of the greyve', a Middle English word for a steward.
namesakes: Dick Grayson (Robin in the Batman comics; surname)

e.etymology: From Aramaic Te'oma, 'twin', the byname of one of the twelve apostles. It grew popular in England after the martyrdom of Thomas Becket in 1170.
namesakes: Thomas the Apostle (the doubting Thomas of the Gospels)

assoc.t: Thomas the Tank Engine
doubting Thomas, a skeptic who needs proof
Thomas' English muffins

e.etymology: From the English name of the purple flower, from Old French violete and Latin viola. One of the flower names taken up for girls in the 19th century, sometimes as an English form of French Violette.
namesakes: Violet Beauregarde (gum chewer in Willy Wonka)

assoc.t: violet, the flower and the purple color

e.etymology: From Hebrew Yitzchak, 'he will laugh', recalling Sarah's laughter when told she would bear a son in old age. Isaac is the son of Abraham and father of Jacob and Esau.
From Spanish Sant Iago, 'Saint James', the apostle said to be buried at Santiago de Compostela. Iago is an old Spanish form of Jacob.
namesakes: Santiago (the fisherman of Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea)

assoc.t: Santiago, capital of Chile
Santiago de Compostela, Spanish pilgrimage city

e.etymology: From Antonius, a Roman family name of unknown, probably Etruscan, origin; the h crept in through a false link to Greek anthos, 'flower'. Saint Anthony the Great and Saint Anthony of Padua spread it.
